title: Data-driven Processes Work for Students, and Schools Should Think About Why
author: Sustainable Schools
summary: Sustainable Schools examines the counterintuitive research finding that structured, data-driven identification systems like Multi-Tiered Systems of Support (MTSS) outperform experienced teachers' own judgment at identifying students who need intervention. The article's central puzzle is why this works, since teachers spend far more time observing students than any screener does; its answer, borrowed from economist Douglass North's theory of institutions, is that MTSS functions as a decision-making institution that reduces transaction costs by standardizing the menu of possible interventions rather than requiring each teacher to invent a bespoke response for every struggling student. The piece argues teachers actually have too much information to reliably isolate the signal relevant to a specific problem, whereas a screener is deliberately designed to ignore everything irrelevant. It closes by generalizing the lesson beyond formal MTSS: individual classrooms and principals can build their own systematic thresholds and pathways, since scale, not perfect personalization, is what most schools actually need to serve every student who requires support.
points: Cites research (VanDerHeyden and Witt, 2005) showing teachers are less accurate than data-driven screening processes at identifying students who need intervention, despite having vastly more observational data than any screener.

Explains the mechanism through economist Douglass North's theory of institutions: MTSS reduces the 'transaction costs' of decision-making by giving teachers a standardized menu of interventions instead of requiring a bespoke response invented for each student.

Argues the paradox is that having more information can make simple identification tasks harder, since zeroing in on the relevant signal is more difficult than relying on a screener 'designed to ignore everything else not relevant to the task.'

Generalizes the lesson beyond formal MTSS: individual classrooms and principals can build their own systematic thresholds and pathways to get more students support at scale, even without adopting schoolwide MTSS.
quotes: It turns out teachers are not as good as data-driven processes at identifying students for intervention. Why is this? After all, teachers are in the classroom with these students hours every week observing them, instructing them, answering their questions. They would have much more data than any universal screener ever could.

But relatively simple tasks can become more difficult the more data there is. Teachers have so much information that zeroing in on the part that is relevant to a particular problem can prove harder than simply relying on a screener that is designed to ignore everything else not relevant to the task.

Institutions are the humanly devised constraints imposed on human interaction. They consist of formal rules, informal constraints and the enforcement characteristics of both. Institutions are important because they reduce the cost of doing business, including the business of helping students succeed.

It's not on the teacher to identify students based on their own observations. A teacher no longer has to come up with novel ways to support students. The supports might be individualized, but the interventions are standardized.

Systems are largely good for students. If each of the steps from identification to intervention has to be created anew for each student, fewer students get support. Systems are not perfect, but they are pretty good at delivering at scale.
